svg.title: Where the Encoders Actually Are
svg.desc: Robot photograph © Pololu Corporation — pololu.com. A RoboLore instructional graphic showing the underside of the Zumo 32U4. Each encoder uses an external magnet disc on the motor's rear shaft plus nearby Hall-effect sensors on the main board. The authentic 800 by 671 pixel PNG is embedded byte-for-byte with two editable vector callouts identifying the left and right encoder areas.
svg.text: ROBOLORE · LESSON 6 · §4
Where the Encoders Actually Are
GRAPHIC 6.6
ENCODER MAGNETS SIT OUTSIDE THE MOTOR CANS
Bottom view — each side uses a rear-shaft magnet disc and nearby Hall sensors.
READING BOTH ENCODERS
encoders.getCountsLeft();
encoders.getCountsRight();
// two numbers, not one
Drive straight and the two counts
should climb together.
If one wheel slips, drags, or hits
a crumb, its count falls behind —
and the robot has silently curved.
Watch one encoder and you will
never see it happen.
This is why we average both.
An encoder cannot see the floor, the wall,
or the line. It only knows
how far its own wheel turned.
A COUNT IS NOT A DISTANCE
The encoder reports turning. It has no idea whether the wheel was gripping the floor or spinning in place.
Lift the robot off the table and drive: the counts climb happily. The robot goes nowhere.
Encoders measure the WHEEL, not the WORLD.
Everything in this lesson depends on the wheel not slipping.
Robot photograph © Pololu Corporation — pololu.com
